S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with onset typically within three months of the stressor and resulting in distress or impairment that is out of proportion to what would be expected. The disturbance causes clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning but does not meet criteria for another specific mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a preexisting condition. Symptoms are time-limited and usually resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, although they can persist if the stressor is ongoing. Clinically, it is differentiated from normal stress reactions by the degree of functional impairment and from disorders like major depression or anxiety disorders by its tighter temporal relationship to a stressor and generally milder, more situational course.

patient.stressor: Roughly a month before seeking help, Gilda’s primary source of income—a series of pop-up art events sponsored by a local gallery—was abruptly canceled when the gallery closed under new ownership, leaving her without the modest but steady payments she relied on to cover rent and studio supplies. Because she tends to manage money informally and sometimes forgets bills, the sudden loss of income led to late notices, mounting fees, and a tense meeting with her landlord about possible eviction if she fell further behind. As she scrambled to design new freelance offerings and apply for part-time work outside her creative field, she found that the financial pressure was starting to overshadow her usual sense of calm curiosity, and she began avoiding her sketching circles and gallery visits because they reminded her of the stalled career plans. When a close friend pointed out how unlike herself she seemed and offered to go with her, Gilda agreed to consult a clinician, worried that her reactions to the financial setback were starting to interfere with her ability to function day to day.
patient.chief_complaint: “Losing that gallery income has thrown me off so much that I feel like I’m not handling the money stress in a normal way anymore.”
